records.place: Casa Branca, in the Alentejo, Portugal

wine.name: Mouchão
wine.grapes: Alicante Bouschet, the great majority, with Trincadeira for the rest.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards at Casa Branca, grown and bottled at Mouchão; the oldest plot is of Alicante Bouschet, the grape the family is thought to have brought from France.
wine.making: Picked by hand and trodden by foot twice a day in the stone lagares of the winery built in 1901, through a fermentation of four to seven days. After the malolactic in large wooden tonéis of five thousand litres, the wine rests about three years before bottling, then two to three years more in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Deep garnet; dark plum, black olive and the stemmy, minty note the house calls its own, turning with age towards dried fig, leather and tar. Firm, generous tannin and a dry, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Released only after years in cask and bottle, it is firm even then, and its tannin is built to carry it for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The estate's red, first labelled under that name with the harvest of 1954.
The Alentejo's appellation, which the house's own sheets give for this wine.
A large estate of the Alentejo, here the family's estate of cork oak and vine.

records.table: Mouchão is the red of Herdade do Mouchão: mostly Alicante Bouschet, trodden by foot in stone lagares and rested about three years in large old casks before years more in bottle. Dark plum, black olive and mint over firm tannin, it wants decanting.
records.story: The Reynolds family came to the Alentejo for cork: by the house's own account its forebear moved there around 1832, drawn by the cork trade, and Mouchão, by Casa Branca, was one of the estates where the family worked the cork oaks. There were probably vines there already. In the early 1890s a grandson of the founder of the cork business built the family house and the farm buildings, and in 1901 came the winery, its stone lagares and its layout little changed since. The family is thought to have brought the first Alicante Bouschet vines from France, and that grape, red in its flesh as well as its skin, became the heart of the estate. For decades the wine was sold in bulk; the first bottling came in 1949, and the Mouchão label was born with the harvest of 1954. After the revolution of 1974 the estate was expropriated, and it came back to the family only in 1986, run down, to be restored by a daughter of the family, her husband and a grandson. Mouchão is the Alentejo before modern winemaking: grapes trodden by foot, years in large old wood, and a red that asks for patience.

others.name: Dom Rafael
others.note: The second label: Alentejo grapes in a softer red, readier in youth than Mouchão.

others.name: Mouchão Tonel 3 and 4
others.note: Alicante Bouschet alone from the Carrapetos vineyard, aged at least three years in the two great casks numbered three and four, then two in bottle.

traps: Tonel 3 and 4 is Alicante Bouschet alone, aged in two numbered casks; the flagship Mouchão is Alicante Bouschet blended with Trincadeira.
Mouchão is trodden in stone lagares and aged in large wooden tonéis; the clay talhas of the Alentejo are a separate tradition.
Alicante Bouschet is a teinturier, a grape whose flesh and juice are red as well as its skin.

cards.front: Herdade do Mouchão: when was its first wine bottled, and when did the Mouchão label begin?
cards.back: Wine was sold in bulk until 1949, when the first was bottled; the Mouchão label began with the harvest of 1954.

cards.front: Which grape makes up most of Mouchão, and what sets it apart?
cards.back: Alicante Bouschet, a teinturier whose flesh and juice are red, with Trincadeira beside it.

questions.q: A guest asks how Herdade do Mouchão makes its red, Mouchão. Which answer fits?
opts: Trodden by foot in stone lagares, then years in large tonéis
Fermented in clay talhas, then sealed under olive oil
Steel tanks, then a year in new French barrels
Whole bunches under carbon dioxide in concrete vats
questions.exp: Mouchão is trodden by foot in the stone lagares of the winery of 1901 and rests about three years in large wooden tonéis; talha wine is a separate Alentejo tradition.

questions.q: Herdade do Mouchão was expropriated after the revolution of 1974. In which year did it come back to the family?
questions.exp: By the house's own account the estate returned to the family only in 1986, run down, and was then restored; 1954 is the first harvest under the Mouchão label.

report: Searches for this record: 9 of the group's 39, four on the house's own domain (mouchao.pt) and one on the CVRA's (vinhosdoalentejo.pt), each read as primary through its summary; no fetch tried.

The dates are the house's History page: the forebear's move around 1832, the house and farm buildings of the early 1890s, the winery of 1901, the first bottling of 1949, the first Mouchão label with the harvest of 1954, the expropriation after 1974 and the return in 1986; one merchant gives 1985 for the return, and the house's 1986 is kept.

No member of the family is named: the house names the forebear, the builder of the 1890s and the first bottler, but no dates were found for any of them, and the restorers of 1986 and the sixth generation are living.

The library's wine note and the plan's why say Mouchão is made only in accepted years; no source searched names a year the red was not made and one merchant calls it the regular reference wine, so the record does not say it, while Tonel 3 and 4 is the wine made only in great years by Decanter and Entrée Cuvée.

The library calls Tonel 3-4 a single-cask bottling from the estate's oldest wood; the house's own sheet racks it into two casks of five thousand litres, numbers 3 and 4, from the Carrapetos vineyard, so the record says two casks, and writes the name Tonel 3 and 4 because the build refuses a hyphen between figures.

The grapes are written the great majority Alicante Bouschet: the house's sheets give 85 and 15 per cent for the 2015 and over 70 per cent for the 2012; the appellation is DOC Alentejo by the house's sheets for the 2012 to 2016 reds.

The coming of Alicante Bouschet is hedged: the CVRA says the family is thought to have imported the first vines from France, one merchant says cuttings from Montpellier in the 1870s and another the end of the nineteenth century; the place is Casa Branca alone, its parish of Sousel resting on one listing (Time Out).
Living names met, none in the prose: the daughter and son-in-law who restored the estate after 1986 and the sixth generation named by the house and its merchants.

wine.name: Pêra-Manca Tinto
wine.grapes: Aragonez and Trincadeira, from vines more than thirty years old.
wine.sites: Old vines of the Évora sub-region of the DOC Alentejo, more than thirty years old, chosen in each year by the house for grapes that ripened slowly and without excess stress.
wine.making: Fermented at a controlled temperature in large vats of French oak, then left on its skins in a long maceration after fermentation. It ages eighteen months in French oak casks of three thousand litres and then, by the house's sheet, some four years in bottle in the cellars of the Cartuxa monastery before release.
wine.glass: Ripe blackberry and redcurrant with raisin, liquorice and black pepper, then cocoa and tobacco as it opens; full bodied, with firm, grainy tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: It is released young, after years in cask and bottle; the house speaks of great longevity, and it needs years more to show its depth.
wine.serve: 17 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The name the foundation keeps for its exceptional wines, bottled only in the years it judges fit.
The charitable foundation of Évora, set up in 1963, whose Cartuxa winery makes the wine.
The Alentejo's appellation, in its sub-region round the city of Évora.

records.table: Pêra-Manca Tinto is the red the Fundação Eugénio de Almeida of Évora bottles only in years it judges fit: Aragonez and Trincadeira from old vines, eighteen months in large French oak casks, then years in the monastery's cellars. Full and firm, it wants a long decanting.
records.story: The name is older than the wine. In the nineteenth century a farming house of Évora made a wine called Pêra-Manca, and Portuguese writers like to tell, as legend, that the navigator who reached Brazil in 1500 carried a wine of that name in his ships. The farming house later ceased trading. The Fundação Eugénio de Almeida was set up on 25 September 1963, endowed by an engineer of that family as a private charitable foundation, and its wines are made at the Cartuxa winery, named for the Carthusian monks of the monastery of Santa Maria Scala Coeli outside the city; the first Cartuxa Reserva came in 1987. In the late 1980s an heir of the old farming house offered the Pêra-Manca name to the foundation, on the condition, as the press tells it, that it be kept for the exceptional wine made there. The first Pêra-Manca of the foundation followed in 1990, and the red has since been bottled only in the years the house judges worthy, after eighteen months in large casks and years in the monastery's cellars. For a sommelier, Pêra-Manca is the Alentejo's red of occasion, and its vintages are read one by one.

others.name: Cartuxa Reserva Tinto
others.note: Alicante Bouschet, Aragonez and Cabernet Sauvignon, first made in 1987 and aged in new French oak barrels.

traps: Pêra-Manca is the wine, Cartuxa the winery that makes it and the Fundação Eugénio de Almeida the charitable foundation behind both; the Cartuxa Reserva is a different wine.
Pêra-Manca red is not made every year: the house bottles it only when it judges a vintage fit, so a missing year on a list is no gap.
The navigator's voyage of 1500 is a legend of the name; the Pêra-Manca of the foundation dates from the vintage of 1990.

cards.front: Pêra-Manca Tinto: which two grapes, and how is it aged?
cards.back: Aragonez and Trincadeira; eighteen months in large French oak casks, then about four years in bottle in the monastery's cellars.

cards.front: In which year did the Fundação Eugénio de Almeida make its first Pêra-Manca?
cards.back: 1990, after an heir of the old farming house of the name offered it to the foundation in the late 1980s.

questions.q: A guest orders Pêra-Manca Tinto and asks what is in the bottle. Which pair of grapes is right?
opts: Aragonez and Trincadeira
Antão Vaz and Arinto
Touriga Nacional and Syrah
Alicante Bouschet and Cabernet Sauvignon
questions.exp: The red is Aragonez and Trincadeira from old vines near Évora; Alicante Bouschet and Cabernet Sauvignon belong to the Cartuxa Reserva, and Antão Vaz and Arinto are white grapes.

questions.q: How did the Fundação Eugénio de Almeida come to own the name Pêra-Manca?
opts: An heir of the old farming house offered it
It bought the name at a public auction
The Carthusian monks gave it to the winery
The state granted it with the DOC Alentejo
questions.exp: In the late 1980s an heir of the farming house that had made Pêra-Manca offered the name to the foundation; the monks gave the winery its name, Cartuxa, not the wine its own.

report: Searches for this record: 11 of the group's 39, four on cartuxa.pt, each read as primary through its summary; not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not in the region record's producers line.
The founding of 25 September 1963 is Decree-Law 108/82 on the Diário da República; the founder is described, not named, because his dates were found in no source searched.

The cession of the name: Agroportal gives 1987, by an heir of the extinct Casa Soares, and another account 1989, so the record says the late 1980s; the condition that the name mark the exceptional wine is Observador's and is hedged as the press's.

The navigator of 1500 is told as legend and not named, for want of his dates in a source read; the gold medals of Bordeaux, the seventy silent years and the reading of the name as a wobbling stone rest on one source each and are left out.

Grapes, vines over thirty years, fermentation in French oak vats, eighteen months in casks of three thousand litres, forty eight months in bottle in the monastery's cellars, release only in fit years and 17 degrees Celsius are the house's sheets for the 2018 and 2019; the glass joins the house's raisin to merchants' notes (Garrafeira Pepe, Vinogrande, 1001 Vinhos), none of them among the five sources.

Sourced but left out for want of room among five sources: the founder's return of the Carthusian monks to Scala Coeli in 1960 (the foundation's own brochure and an academic paper) and their departure in 2019 (RTP, Diário de Notícias); the monastery's date is left out because the house's sheets give 1598 in one and 1587 in another.

The Pêra-Manca white (Antão Vaz and Arinto, first made in 1990 by the house's white sheets) is left out of others for the same reason; the plan's note is answered: the first red of 1990, the older story as legend, and the Cartuxa Reserva in others.
Living names met, none in the prose: the winemaking team Observador names and the foundation's executives.

records.place: Reguengos de Monsaraz, DOC Alentejo, Alentejo

wine.name: Esporão Reserva Tinto
wine.grapes: A blend of Alicante Bouschet, Aragonez, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon, with Touriga Nacional in later vintages.
wine.sites: Grapes of the Herdade do Esporão alone, by the regional commission's record, from vineyards near Reguengos de Monsaraz on granite with seams of schist and a clay loam structure.
wine.making: Each grape is destemmed, crushed and fermented apart at a controlled temperature in stainless steel vats, concrete tanks and small marble lagares, with the malolactic in steel. The blend then ages twelve months in American and French oak barrels, most of them used, and at least six months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Intense ruby; blackberry, wild berries and ripe plum with cinnamon and liquorice. Rich and dense in the mouth, with robust tannin and a fresh, persistent finish.
wine.ageing: By the house's own notes it has the tannin and density to gain from some years in bottle.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The house's first wine, made since the harvest of 1985 from the estate's own grapes.
The estate by Reguengos de Monsaraz whose bounds, by its own account, were fixed in 1267.
The region of origin, the wine listed with the Alentejo's regional wine commission.

records.table: Esporão Reserva has been the red of Herdade do Esporão since its first harvest of 1985: Alicante Bouschet, Aragonez, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon from the estate by Reguengos, a year in oak. Each vintage carries a different artist's work on its label.
records.story: Herdade do Esporão is far older than its wine. By the house's account its bounds were fixed in 1267, when it was the Defesa do Esporão, and have hardly moved since; the Reconquista had taken Monsaraz and Reguengos in 1232. Its tower, raised in the fifteenth century by a holder of the entailed estate, stands on the estate, and the Counts of Alcáçovas held the land until 1973. That year two partners bought it, founding the company that carries its name. After the revolution of April 1974 the estate was occupied in the land reform, and only in 1985 did it give the harvest of its first wine, Esporão Reserva red. With that wine came a custom: each year an invited artist, almost always Portuguese, makes the work that fills its label, a painting on the first of them. A winery was built in 1987, the wines went abroad from 1989, and in 2000 came a second winery, the Adega dos Lagares, and the first Private Selection red. For a sommelier, Esporão Reserva is the Alentejo's own grapes blended with Cabernet Sauvignon, under a label that has been a gallery since 1985.

others.name: Esporão Reserva Branco
others.note: The white Reserva of the house, made beside the red.

others.name: Esporão Private Selection Tinto
others.note: The red first made under that name in 2000, grown from the house's earlier Garrafeira.

traps: Esporão Reserva, first made in 1985, is the house's first wine; the Private Selection, from 2000, is a different and later red.
The painting on an Esporão Reserva label changes with every vintage, so a new label is no new wine.
Herdade do Esporão lies in the Reguengos sub-region of the Alentejo, not in Évora or Borba.

cards.front: Herdade do Esporão: which wine was the first it made, and from which harvest?
cards.back: Esporão Reserva red, from the harvest of 1985.

cards.front: What sets each new label of Esporão Reserva apart from the last?
cards.back: A new work by an invited artist each year, a custom since the first vintage of 1985.

questions.q: A guest asks how Esporão Reserva red is aged before it reaches the table. Which answer fits?
opts: Twelve months in American and French oak barrels
Three years in large old tonéis of chestnut
Six months in clay talhas under olive oil
No wood at all, only stainless steel
questions.exp: The house ages the blend a year in American and French barrels, most of them used, then at least six months in bottle; talhas belong to the Alentejo's older tradition.

questions.q: Esporão's first wine came from the harvest of 1985. Which custom began with it?
opts: An artist's new work on each label
A label printed on a sheet of cork
A name that hides the grape
A release only in exceptional years
questions.exp: Since 1985 an invited artist has made the work on each Esporão Reserva label; the cork label is Adega de Borba's and the hidden grape is Cortes de Cima's Incógnito.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 39, five on esporao.com and one on the CVRA's, each read as primary through its summary; not in WINE_PRODUCERS.

The bounds of 1267, the Reconquista of 1232, the tower of the fifteenth century (1457 to 1490 by the house), the Counts of Alcáçovas until 1973, the purchase of 1973, the occupation after April 1974, the first harvest of 1985, the winery of 1987, exports from 1989 and the Adega dos Lagares and Private Selection of 2000 are the house's own history pages.
The return of the estate is not dated: Blend gives 1978, a travel guide has the work resume with planting in 1979, and the house says only that it was occupied, so the record says neither.

The artists' labels since 1985 are the house's; the first was by a painter whose dates were not searched, so he is not named, and the house counts 29 Portuguese, one Brazilian and two Angolan artists by 2015, hence almost always Portuguese.

Grapes: the CVRA's older sheet gives Alicante Bouschet, Aragonez, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon, the house's 2021 and 2022 add Touriga Nacional, and the 2019 and 2020 pages Syrah or Touriga Franca, so the record names the four and Touriga Nacional in later vintages; the oak is a fifth new in 2021 and 2022, and the older sheet gives 70 per cent American.
The appellation field says Alentejo alone: no source read named DOC Alentejo or Regional Alentejano for this wine, so the checker may settle it from a label.
The plan's note is answered: the founding of 1973, the first Reserva of 1985 and the grapes in words; the white Reserva is in others.
Living names met, none in the prose: the two founding partners (one living, the other's status unknown), the founder's son and the long serving winemaker.

records.place: Borba, in the Borba sub-region of DOC Alentejo

wine.name: Adega de Borba Reserva Tinto
wine.grapes: A blend of Aragonez, Trincadeira, Castelão and Alicante Bouschet.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the Borba sub-region on clay limestone and schist soils, by the house's own sheet.
wine.making: Made only in years the co-operative judges exceptional. After the malolactic fermentation in stainless steel, the wine ages twelve months in French oak barrels in their third and fourth year and in large casks of exotic wood, then six months in bottle in the cellar before release.
wine.glass: Clear ruby with red glints; jammy dark berries and a hint of white chocolate, fine rather than heavy. Soft and balanced in the mouth, with ripe, structured tannin, a slight grip and an elegant finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release, it can be kept, by the house's account, for ten years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 17 degrees Celsius, as the regional commission advises; decant an older bottle gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The cork label, made of cork itself, first used for the vintage of 1964 in homage to the Alentejo's cork.
Here the co-operative's red made only in the years it judges exceptional.
The Alentejo's appellation, in its sub-region round the town of Borba.

records.table: Adega de Borba Reserva, the red the Borba co-operative has dressed in a label of cork since its vintage of 1964, blends Aragonez, Trincadeira, Castelão and Alicante Bouschet and spends a year in oak. Soft and balanced, it is made only in years judged exceptional.
records.story: Adega de Borba is a co-operative. Its first board took office on 30 April 1955, and by its own account it was the first of a series of co-operative wineries set up across the Alentejo with the support of the Junta Nacional do Vinho, the national wine board of the time. The growers of Borba brought their grapes to one shared cellar. In 1964 the co-operative made the first vintage of its Reserva red and dressed it in a label made of cork, in homage, as the house tells it, to the Alentejo's other harvest, the bark of its cork oaks. The wine became known by its label: the house's own pages call its Reserva the Rótulo de Cortiça, the cork label. It has been made since only in the years the co-operative judges exceptional, so that the vintage of 2018 was only the twenty fifth edition of the wine. For a sommelier, the cork label teaches two things: that a co-operative's red can be made to keep for a decade, and that a label can become a wine's name.

others.name: Adega de Borba Grande Reserva Tinto
others.note: The co-operative's Grande Reserva red, sold under a label of cork as well.

others.name: Adega de Borba Reserva Branco
others.note: The white Reserva, sold under the cork label beside the red.

traps: The cork label is the Reserva's dress, first used for the vintage of 1964; it is not a separate wine from Adega de Borba Reserva.
Adega de Borba is a co-operative of the town's growers founded in 1955, not a single family estate.
Borba is a sub-region of the DOC Alentejo, so the label reads Alentejo with Borba beside it.

cards.front: Adega de Borba: what is the Rótulo de Cortiça, and when did it begin?
cards.back: The cork label of its Reserva red, first used for the vintage of 1964 in homage to the Alentejo's cork.

cards.front: In which year did the Borba co-operative's first board take office?
cards.back: 1955, on 30 April; by its own account the first of a series of co-operative wineries across the Alentejo.

questions.q: A guest asks which grapes go into Adega de Borba Reserva, the cork label red. Which answer fits?

Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz
Syrah alone, from vines near Vidigueira
Baga with a little Touriga Nacional

questions.q: Adega de Borba first dressed its Reserva in a label of cork. In which vintage?
questions.exp: The first vintage under the cork label was 1964, nine years after the co-operative's first board took office in 1955.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 39, two on adegaborba.pt and one on the CVRA's, each read as primary through its summary; not in WINE_PRODUCERS.

The first board of 30 April 1955 and the first of a series of Alentejo co-operative wineries with the Junta Nacional do Vinho are the house's History page; the first cork label vintage of 1964, the homage to cork and exceptional years only are its press pages, and the 2018 as twenty fifth edition its own article.
The house's pages call the brand more than fifty years old and an older article more than forty five, both consistent with 1964.

Grapes, clay limestone and schist soils, twelve months in French barrels of third and fourth use and in exotic wood casks, and six months in bottle are the house's page for the 2022; 16 to 17 degrees Celsius and DOC Borba are the CVRA's page; the glass is the house's note, its dark fruit written as jammy dark berries.

The plan's why says the Reserva taught a generation of Portuguese what an Alentejo red tastes like, and the region record's line says the same; no source read says it, so the record does not; the marble country of the why is not sourced either and is left out.

Others: the Grande Reserva under a cork label and the Reserva Branco are on the house's own shop pages (adegaborba.pt/loja/rotulo-cortica-grande-reserva/ and adegaborba.pt/loja/produto/rotulo-de-cortica-branco/), not among the five sources for want of room.
Living names met, none in the prose: the co-operative's chief executive quoted in its press pages.

wine.name: Incógnito
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards near Vidigueira, the first of them planted in 1991, Syrah among them, when the grape was not yet allowed in the Alentejo.
wine.making: By the house's sheet for the 2021, the grapes are picked by hand at night and fermented with their own yeasts, half of them as whole bunches, with some two and a half weeks on the skins and a gentle extraction, then aged six months in used barrels of five hundred litres.
wine.glass: Deep in colour, with blackberry and plum over black pepper, smoke and a toasted note; powerful and peppery in the mouth, with firm tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Powerful and firm when young, it is made to age and gains from several years in bottle.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large red wine glass.

label.means: In disguise: the name of a Syrah first made when the grape was not allowed in the Alentejo.
The Alentejo's regional wine, the category the house uses for this wine rather than the DOC.
The farm near Vidigueira that its founders found in 1988 and planted with vines.

records.table: Incógnito is Cortes de Cima's Syrah from Vidigueira, named in disguise because the grape was not yet allowed in the Alentejo when its first vintage, 1998, was made. Blackberry, plum and black pepper over firm tannin: decant it for an hour.
records.story: Cortes de Cima was a farm of old olives, cereals and animals near Vidigueira when a Danish and American couple, who had reached Portugal by sailing boat, found it in 1988, with an old house that had neither electricity nor running water. They grew melons and dried tomatoes at first, and in 1991 planted vines, Syrah among them, though the grape was not then allowed in the Alentejo. The first harvest came in 1996. With the vintage of 1998 the Syrah was bottled on its own, and since its grape could not be named, the wine went out as Incógnito; by the house's account that first vintage won a gold medal at a competition in Brussels. Its success, the house says, helped force a change in the rules, and Syrah was later admitted, so that Alentejo labels came to carry its name. In 2019 the founders' daughter took the estate on and turned it from a single crop towards mixed farming. For a sommelier, Incógnito is the story of a grape that came into the Alentejo by the side door, and a reminder that a wine's name can record a law.

others.name: Cortes de Cima Tinto
others.note: The estate's red under its own name, from its vineyards near Vidigueira.

others.name: Chaminé
others.note: A red and a white of the estate under a name of their own.

Cortes de Cima planted its Syrah in 1991, but Incógnito's first vintage is 1998, not the year of planting.

cards.front: Which grape is Incógnito, and where does it grow?
cards.back: Syrah alone, from Cortes de Cima's vineyards near Vidigueira.

questions.q: A guest asks under which category Cortes de Cima labels Incógnito. Which answer fits?
opts: Vinho Regional Alentejano
DOC Alentejo, sub-region Vidigueira
DOC Alentejo, sub-region Portalegre
Vinho de Talha DOC Alentejo
questions.exp: Incógnito is labelled Vinho Regional Alentejano, the regional wine the house uses rather than the DOC; Vidigueira is where it grows, not its category.

questions.q: Cortes de Cima planted Syrah in 1991 near Vidigueira. What did the rules of the day mean for its first wine?
opts: Its grape could not be named on the label
It had to be blended with Aragonez and Trincadeira
It could be sold only to the local co-operative
It had to be aged in clay talhas
questions.exp: Syrah was not yet allowed in the Alentejo, so the 1998 went out as Incógnito with no grape named; the house says its success helped change the rules.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 39, two on the house's domains and one on the CVRA's; not in WINE_PRODUCERS.

The founding year 1988 rests on Wine Disclosures and a merchant's history (Wine and Earth), the house itself saying only the 1980s; the farm, the boat, the vines of 1991, the first harvest of 1996 and the daughter's taking on the estate in 2019 are the house's own pages.
The 1998 Incógnito born an outlaw, and its gold medal in Brussels, are the house's, the medal hedged; that Syrah was not then allowed is the house's and Wine Disclosures'.

The year Syrah was admitted was found nowhere: the Portarias of 2010 and 2014 only restate the lists, so the plan's note goes unanswered and the record says later, borne out by the CVRA's listing of Syrah varietals as Regional Alentejano.

The making is the house's sheet for the 2021, dated as such: the wine changed after 2019 to whole bunches, used barrels of five hundred litres and lower alcohol, while older vintages were reviewed as powerful (Wine Enthusiast), so the checker should weigh whether the glass and ageing, drawn from those reviews and merchants (Portugal Get Wine, Firstleaf), fit the later wine.
One account says the first label carried neither grape nor vintage and that the back label spelt Syrah in initials; one source only, left out.
Others: Cortes de Cima Tinto and Chaminé red and white are on the house's sheets and the CVRA's producer page, not among the five sources.
Living names met, none in the prose: the two founders and their daughter.
